newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-Veteran London dealers regret loss of long lunches.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Veteran London dealers regret loss of long lunches.

text.p: London's centuries old financial district is on the threshold of a new age as both a fledgling Labour government and European economic union make their mark.
And it is not just bank balance sheets that must adjust, say veteran traders. Time-worn traditions that have survived the explosion of technology are also under threat.

"Certainly the chances of having a decent lunch with port and a cigar are few and far between now," said a trader who has been in the business nearly 35 years. "We used to have them three or four times a week -- now it seems lunch is for wimps." Long lunches are not the only casualties. Christy of London, the city's most celebrated hat factory, faces closure after more than 200 years of business. It seems there is little demand any more for the trilbys and bowler hats City gents used to favour.

The trend towards a leaner, slicker market place, some say, has even been given added impetus from Prime Minister Tony Blair's more relaxed approach to government since Labour trouced the Conservatives at the beginning of May.

Gordon Brown, holder of the venerable post of Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) wore a plain business suit to the annual "Mansion House" address on the economy with the Lord Mayor of London in June instead of the usual formal black or even white tie.
This alone was enough to raise the hackles of some City diehards.
"Some people like to hang on to old traditions -- and some of those in the City are dearly cherished," the veteran trader sighed.
"It's unheard of to go to the Mansion House in anything less than a dinner jacket. It is like the Queen going to the state opening of parliament in wellington boots."
The hundreds of banks and brokerages packed into the narrow streets of the area known as the City have been bombarded with reforms in the first weeks of Labour rule.
And as Europe's cities jostle for prime position with the approach of monetary union, City powerhouses should ready themselves for further upheaval, industry watchers say.
"We're in for some more lean times," said Stephen Lewis, director of London Bond Broking and a money man for 27 years.
"We're building up globally to a period where the phenomenal expansion in financial markets of the last 20 years will come to a halt or even reverse."
With the size of the financial pie potentially shrinking, some worry London will get a smaller piece.
"If the euro gets off the ground, it will inevitably inhibit turnover in financial markets because some business involves switches between what will be unified currencies," said Lewis.
He predicted a bout of staff lay-offs and a move to more defensive investment strategies would follow.
But it's not all doom and gloom.
"London's a long, long way ahead of anyone else in our time zone, and I think we'll keep that position," said Lewis.
MOVING WITH THE TIMES
London has a history of adapting to change -- one which will stand it in good stead for the turmoil ahead.
The speed at which prices and information zip through City trading rooms today is a far cry from the Dickensian days when top-hatted gentlemen crouched over dusty ledgers.
Even 30 years ago the City was a very different place than it is now. For instance, then it was of unheard of for price moves to hinge on events outside Britain.

"Overseas markets had no influence whatsoever," said the veteran trader. "Nobody cared about an interest rate rise in the U.S. or Germany, and certainly nobody was on tenterhooks about something like the 'Philadelphia Fed Index'."
The City's real coming of age was in 1982 when the futures market opened.
"That showed that overseas players were really having an influence on things," said the trader.
"Big Bang" in 1986 was the next milestone for London markets, when electronic trading was introduced and many antiquated dealing systems were abolished.
That and the share market crash in 1987 marked the end of the affluent '80s when pay packets bulged and it was fashionable to "pay and display."

Ten years of relative stability followed as a City-friendly Conservative government largely left markets to their own devices. Multi-million-pound disasters such as the collapses of Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) and Barings prompted regulatory reviews, but no sea-change in the City environment.
LABOUR SETS A BLISTERING PACE
So how will the City fare under Labour?
Britain's markets cautiously applauded the move to Labour rule. The two had uneasy relations in the past. The City frowned on Labour's old tax and spend ways and felt the party lacked market savvy.

But pre-election promises to keep a tight rein on inflation and spending reassured some of the more sceptical that Labour has learned its lesson. That, plus dramatic reforms to the Bank of England and City regulation, has given the market plenty to digest for the time being.
"There is a danger that if Labour continues to initiate reforms at the pace it has been... then people will accuse it of doing too much too quickly," said Philip Shaw, UK economist at Union Plc.
"But if you consider the changes made so far on their own merits, they do indeed on the whole seem very, very sensible."

Labour handed operational control of interest rates over to the Bank of England within days of coming to power, and late in May said a new, beefier Securities and Investments Board would take on most financial market regulation.
Shaw said Labour may have more reforms up its sleeve -- 18 years in opposition is a long time to mull over policy initiatives.
Some are also wary of the Labour "love-in" and say the honeymoon may soon be over.
"Before long, the City will be looking at Labour with a much more critical eye," said London Bond Broking's Lewis.
"At the moment, there's this New Labour vision...but the love-in going on will come to an end and the government's actions will be viewed much more objectively," he said
He said Labour's first budget, to be announced on Wednesday, may be the turning point, particularly if there is any evidence of the old spendthrift ways.

Brown has already raised a few eyebrows in the City. The Chancellor is traditionally allowed a tipple of choice while presenting the budget to parliament -- former finance minister Norman Lamont sipped gin and tonic, Kenneth Clarke opted for a dram of whisky -- and Brown has elected to enjoy a thirst-quenching mineral water.
